reading.title: Designing What You See and Hear
reading.purpose: Discover how museum designers blend sights and sounds to bring exhibits to life.
paras: Walking into a great museum hall feels smooth and easy. Still, months of hard work sit behind each glass case. Teams blend visual design—what guests see—with auditory design, the layer of sound that sets the mood. The roots vis for seeing and aud for hearing are both at work the moment you step in.

Long before builders raise a single wall, a visionary lead planner must envision how the room will feel months later. Quick sketches and tiny scale models help the team visualize each hall in their minds before they spend a dime on wood or paint.

Light and layout guide the eye. In a nature room, artists might paint a wide mountain vista across a curved wall, giving guests the thrill of standing high above a valley. Meanwhile, crews tuck wires and speakers behind cloth panels so the gear stays invisible to anyone walking past.

Sound needs just as much care. If a voice track is too low, it turns inaudible as soon as a loud class enters the room. Sound crews test each corner so birdsong, footsteps, and short tales stay clearly audible without spilling into the next hall.
When sights and sounds work as one, the audience—the guests gathered in the room—forgets it is inside a city building. People feel swept straight into a rain forest, a ship deck, or an old market.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "inaudible" most nearly means
choices: too loud for visitors in the next gallery room
too quiet to be heard clearly in the space
hidden behind cloth panels along the wall
painted across a wide curved museum backdrop
qs.why: Paragraph 4 links inaudible with a voice that is "too quiet" to hear whenever a school group enters.

qs.q: Which sentence shows how technicians keep equipment from distracting visitors?
choices: Light and layout guide the eye.
Meanwhile, crews tuck wires and speakers behind cloth panels so the gear stays invisible to anyone walking past.
Sound needs just as much care.
People feel swept straight into a rain forest, a ship deck, or an old market.
qs.why: Hiding wires and speakers behind cloth panels keeps the technical gear out of visitors' sight.

ev.text: Meanwhile, crews tuck wires and speakers behind cloth panels so the gear stays invisible to anyone walking past.

qs.q: Why do exhibit teams build tiny scale models before builders start working?
choices: So museum guests can carry small wooden models home from the hall.
So artists do not have to paint curved backdrops on the museum walls.
So planners can picture the room before buying wood or paint.
So sound crews can record birdsong and footsteps inside the models.
qs.why: Paragraph 2 says tiny scale models help the team visualize each hall "before they spend a dime on wood or paint."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Museums feel real because teams plan both sight and sound.
School groups make museum halls far too noisy for recorded voices.
Nature halls are harder to paint than old markets or wooden ship decks.
Most museum planners spend all their time hiding wires behind cloth.
qs.why: The reading explains how visual layout, models, hidden hardware, and balanced sound combine to transport museum guests.
